Before: Strong Mg²⁺–solvent interactions can hinder magnesium deposition, making desolvation a key consideration in electrolyte design. Anions within the first solvation shell can change these interactions and the pathways by which ligands are released. Their contribution therefore extends beyond the formation of an anion-derived solid–electrolyte interphase. In this Perspective, we examine how anion coordination can facilitate Mg²⁺ desolvation and why increased ion pairing is beneficial in some electrolytes but detrimental in others. We discuss how coordination geometry, competing interactions and ligand-exchange dynamics influence the balance between reversible deposition and electrolyte decomposition. Representative studies show the need to distinguish easier ligand release from increased populations of reactive Mg species and improved surface protection. We propose experimental controls and computational approaches to resolve these contributions and establish when a desolvation mechanism applies across electrolyte compositions. Finally, we consider how anion-assisted transfer at the Mg electrode can be reconciled with cathode compatibility and limited electrolyte consumption. This analysis provides a basis for selecting anions that promote desolvation without compromising stability at either electrode.
After: Anion coordination is widely used to tune magnesium electrolytes, yet reversible Mg deposition has been achieved both by increasing and by reducing ion pairing. This apparent contradiction cannot be resolved from the first solvation shell alone. Here, we examine how coordinated anions can assist Mg²⁺ desolvation by changing Mg–solvent interactions and the sequence of ligand rearrangement and release. This molecular role extends beyond their contribution to solid–electrolyte interphase formation. We distinguish changes in the abundance of reactive Mg species from changes in their reactivity, and explain why stable coordination can either enable deposition or hinder it. Representative electrolytes illustrate how these effects coexist with suppressed decomposition and surface protection. We then discuss the measurements needed to connect solvation structure with ligand-exchange kinetics, Mg deposition and anion consumption. Finally, we outline how controlled electrolyte series and interfacial modelling can guide anion selection while accounting for cathode compatibility and limited material inventories. The aim is to establish which desolvation step an anion assists, and under which conditions that benefit survives in a working cell.

Before: 1.1. Why magnesium requires different electrolyte design principles
After: 1.1. Magnesium solvation and interphase chemistry

Before: Reversible magnesium deposition requires an electrolyte that supports ligand rearrangement and Mg reduction without progressively blocking the metal surface. The early rechargeable Mg battery prototype combined an organohaloaluminate electrolyte with a Chevrel-phase cathode.[1–2] Electrochemical studies before and after this demonstration showed that Mg plating/stripping depends strongly on the coordinating solvent and electrode preparation.[3–5] These coupled requirements continue to limit the development of magnesium and other multivalent batteries.[6–9] Understanding how dissolved Mg species undergo desolvation and reduction is therefore essential to improving electrolyte performance beyond a particular formulation.
After: Magnesium electrolyte design must address two connected problems: removing ligands from solvated Mg species and maintaining a surface at which Mg can be deposited and stripped. The early rechargeable Mg battery prototype met these requirements with an organohaloaluminate electrolyte and a Chevrel-phase cathode.[1–2] Electrochemical studies before and after that demonstration showed how strongly Mg plating/stripping depends on the coordinating solvent and electrode preparation.[3–5] The same constraints remain central to magnesium and other multivalent batteries.[6–9] They also explain why a formulation that dissolves a Mg salt readily may still fail to support reversible deposition.

Before: Lithium electrolytes provide useful design principles, but their interphase chemistry cannot be transferred directly to magnesium. In Li systems, salt concentration and anion coordination can alter electrolyte reduction and improve electrode compatibility.[10–15] A functional solid-electrolyte interphase (SEI) suppresses electron leakage while permitting Li-ion transport.[16–17] Many decomposition layers on Mg instead inhibit further plating and stripping, although suitable artificial and electrolyte-derived interphases can sustain cycling.[18–20] Comparisons of Li and Mg highlight these different transport requirements.[21] The presence of a familiar SEI component is consequently insufficient to establish that a film supports Mg transport.
After: Lithium batteries offer useful guidance, but electrolyte decomposition has different consequences for Mg. In Li electrolytes, salt concentration and anion coordination can redirect reduction reactions and improve electrode compatibility.[10–15] A functional solid–electrolyte interphase (SEI) limits electron leakage while allowing Li-ion transport.[16–17] Many decomposition layers on Mg instead block plating and stripping, although suitable artificial and electrolyte-derived interphases can sustain cycling.[18–20] The distinction concerns transport and stability within the operating layer.[21] A component familiar from Li batteries does not, by itself, establish that the layer permits Mg transport.

Before: A hybrid organic/inorganic Mg interphase illustrates the importance of separating solution chemistry from surface protection. The preformed layer continues to suppress side reactions after the electrode is transferred to a TFSI-containing electrolyte.[20] This observation supports a protective role for the retained interphase, but does not explain how solvated Mg releases its ligands in the replacement electrolyte. Solution coordination influences which Mg species reach the electrode, where their reactions also depend on the evolving surface. Efficient deposition may require both favourable ligand exchange and a permeable, chemically stable interphase; evidence for one does not establish the other.
After: A hybrid organic/inorganic Mg interphase illustrates this distinction. After the treated electrode is transferred to a TFSI-containing electrolyte, the preformed layer continues to suppress side reactions.[20] This retained protection establishes a surface contribution. It leaves a molecular question: how does solvated Mg release its ligands in the replacement liquid? Efficient deposition may require favourable ligand exchange and a stable, permeable interphase together; evidence for either contribution cannot establish the other.

Before: Compared with Li⁺, Mg²⁺ generally interacts more strongly with similar donor groups, making ligand exchange sensitive to polarisation, ion association and coordination geometry.[22–23] Ligand denticity also matters: one multidentate molecule can bind through several donor atoms. Direct anion coordination changes the charge and geometry of the Mg complex without changing the formal Mg(II) oxidation state. This interaction can favour ligand rearrangement, but persistent Mg–anion binding may impede subsequent release. Reversible deposition has been achieved both by reducing ion pairing and by promoting selected anion–solvent interactions.[24–25] These results raise a mechanistic question: under what conditions does anion coordination facilitate desolvation?
After: Mg²⁺ generally binds comparable donor groups more strongly than Li⁺, so changes in polarisation, ion association and coordination geometry can have pronounced effects on ligand exchange.[22–23] A multidentate ligand adds another constraint because several donor contacts may have to open before the molecule leaves. When an anion coordinates directly, it changes the charge and geometry of the Mg complex while Mg retains its formal +2 oxidation state. The new coordination environment may facilitate ligand rearrangement or make subsequent release more difficult. Indeed, reversible deposition has been reported after either reducing ion pairing or promoting selected anion–solvent interactions.[24–25] These apparently opposing strategies suggest that the role of the anion must be understood through the reaction it changes.

Before: 1.2. Connecting electrolyte composition with the deposition mechanism
After: 1.2. Limits of a structure-only interpretation

Before: Magnesium electrolytes include organometallic complexes, simple salts and mixtures of coordinating solvents.[26–29] Changing one component can alter ion association, ligand exchange and interfacial reactions simultaneously. Coordination numbers and isolated binding energies describe aspects of the solvation environment, but do not identify the rate-limiting step in deposition.[23,30–31] For example, calculations on chloride-containing Mg complexes suggest that clustering can facilitate desolvation while hindering electron transfer.[32] Chemical equilibria and oxidative stability impose additional constraints.[33] An effective design parameter must therefore describe a specified reaction and predict how that reaction responds to a change in composition or potential.
After: The diversity of Mg electrolytes makes a universal structural descriptor unlikely. Organometallic complexes, simple salts and mixtures of donors generate different equilibria and different interfacial reactants.[26–29] Changing one component can alter ion association, ligand exchange and reduction chemistry together. Coordination numbers and isolated binding energies describe part of this chemistry, but they do not identify the slow step in deposition.[23,30–31] Calculations on chloride-containing Mg complexes, for example, suggest that clustering can facilitate desolvation while hindering electron transfer.[32] Chemical equilibria and oxidative stability impose further constraints.[33] A descriptor becomes useful for design when it is tied to a defined reaction and predicts the response to composition or electrode potential.

Before: The interactions among Mg ions, anions and solvents must be considered together. Organoboron, non-Grignard and alkoxide electrolytes contain chemically distinct Mg species,[34–36] and even changing a substituent can alter the electrochemical behaviour of a Grignard-derived formulation.[37] Comparisons among these families should ask which species participates in deposition, how it loses or rearranges its ligands, and which side reactions compete with Mg reduction. Similar Coulombic efficiencies may arise from different combinations of these processes. Identifying the relevant reaction is what allows a coordination principle established in one electrolyte to guide the design of another.
After: Comparisons between electrolyte families make this requirement clear. Organoboron, non-Grignard and alkoxide formulations contain chemically distinct Mg species,[34–36] and substituent changes affect electrochemistry even within a Grignard-derived family.[37] Similar Coulombic efficiencies may arise from more reactive complexes, faster ligand release or suppressed electrolyte reduction. Distinguishing these contributions determines whether an explanation developed for one formulation can guide another.

Before: 1.3. Anion coordination as a means of facilitating desolvation
After: 1.3. The molecular role of coordinated anions

Before: The central argument of this Perspective is that anions in the first solvation shell should be considered for their ability to assist Mg²⁺ desolvation, beyond their possible role as SEI precursors. Anion coordination can change Mg–solvent interactions, displace a strongly bound donor or favour a configuration from which the remaining ligands are more readily released. Such effects can influence deposition before an electrolyte-derived film forms. Studies of competing coordination, dynamic solvation and interactions beyond the first shell provide evidence and hypotheses for these molecular contributions.[25,38–39] Throughout this article, direct coordination means contact between Mg and a donor atom of the anion. A contact ion pair contains this interaction; in a solvent-separated pair, solvent molecules separate the ions.
After: In this Perspective, we argue that anions in the first solvation shell should be considered for their ability to assist Mg²⁺ desolvation, beyond their role as possible SEI precursors. A coordinated anion can redistribute Mg–ligand interactions, replace a strongly bound solvent or favour a configuration from which ligands can leave more readily. These effects do not require the anion to decompose into a protective film. Studies of competing coordination, dynamic solvation and interactions outside the first shell provide evidence and testable explanations for such molecular contributions.[25,38–39] Here, direct coordination means contact between Mg and a donor atom of the anion. This contact defines a contact ion pair; a solvent-separated pair has intervening solvent molecules.

Before: We examine when anion coordination facilitates ligand removal, when it stabilises a slowly reacting Mg complex, and how these effects can be distinguished from interphase formation. A precursor here is a solvated or interfacial Mg species present before the reaction step under consideration. Its abundance, ligand-exchange rate and tendency to decompose require different measurements. Representative electrolytes illustrate these contributions and guide proposed tests at both electrodes. The aim is to connect anion selection with a defined desolvation mechanism and establish whether it remains applicable when the solvent, salt or operating potential changes.
After: We first consider why weak ion pairing and direct anion coordination can each support reversible Mg deposition. We then examine the measurements that distinguish changes in Mg-species populations, ligand-exchange kinetics and side reactions. A precursor denotes the solvated or interfacial Mg species present before the particular reaction step being considered. This distinction allows the design discussion to move from a preferred shell composition to a specific chemical function. The final sections address how that function can be tested across electrolyte compositions and retained at both electrodes in a working cell.

Before: 2.1. Reducing ion association while retaining accessible solvent exchange
After: 2.1. Weak ion pairing and solvent-controlled desolvation

Before: Weak ion pairing can improve deposition when Mg–anion association limits the supply of reactive Mg species or promotes electrolyte decomposition. A Mg(TFSI)₂ electrolyte designed through solvent selection combines greater ion-pair dissociation with reversible deposition,[24] whereas earlier studies show that TFSI-based electrolytes are sensitive to solvent identity and cycling history.[40–42] Reducing anion coordination, however, leaves the Mg–solvent shell to reorganize before deposition. Solvent exchange and surface reactions can therefore remain limiting even in a well-dissociated electrolyte. Ionic conductivity alone cannot resolve these limitations, because it also depends on viscosity, ion mobility and correlated ion motion.
After: Reducing ion pairing is beneficial when Mg–anion association limits the supply of reactive Mg species or favours decomposition. Solvent selection in a Mg(TFSI)₂ electrolyte has combined greater pair dissociation with reversible deposition,[24] whereas earlier TFSI-based studies show strong dependence on solvent identity and cycling history.[40–42] Dissociation removes one possible constraint, but Mg remains coordinated by solvent. Those ligands must still rearrange or detach during the interfacial reaction. Consequently, a well-dissociated electrolyte can retain slow desolvation or unfavourable surface chemistry. An increase in conductivity cannot establish which constraint has been relieved, because conductivity also reflects viscosity, mobility and correlated ion motion.

Before: Weakly coordinating anions offer another way to reduce Mg–anion association. Boron clusters and carboranes expanded Mg electrolyte chemistry beyond organohalide formulations, with modification improving solubility and stability.[43–46] Fluorinated borates and alkoxyaluminates provided less corrosive, higher-voltage options.[47–51] Bulky anions can still associate with Mg under suitable conditions. Their usefulness depends on reducing detrimental contacts while allowing the remaining solvent ligands to rearrange at the electrode.
After: Weakly coordinating anions offer a chemically distinct route to reducing Mg–anion association. Boron clusters and carboranes expanded the range of Mg electrolytes beyond organohalide formulations; subsequent modifications improved their solubility and stability.[43–46] Fluorinated borates and alkoxyaluminates introduced less corrosive options compatible with higher voltages.[47–51] These advances do not imply complete anion exclusion under every condition. Rather, they show the value of avoiding detrimental association while retaining a solvent environment that permits Mg to react at the electrode.

Before: After persistent Mg–anion contacts are reduced, solvent coordination may limit desolvation. Competitive ethers can loosen a borate solvation environment,[52] while hydrofluoroether–diglyme mixtures also modify Mg coordination.[53] If ion pairing decreases but deposition slows within a controlled series, measurements of solvent exchange, adsorption and surface reactions can identify the remaining constraint. This comparison establishes when further dissociation ceases to improve deposition.
After: Once persistent Mg–anion contacts are reduced, solvent exchange becomes a design target. Competitive ethers can loosen a borate solvation environment,[52] and hydrofluoroether–diglyme mixtures also modify Mg coordination.[53] If anion contacts decrease while deposition slows in a controlled series, another step has become restrictive. Solvent-exchange, adsorption and surface measurements can identify it. Further dissociation is then useful only if it relieves that remaining constraint.

Before: Comparisons of carborane- and TFSI-based electrolytes examine the evolving Mg/electrolyte interface alongside anion identity.[54] Initial solvation structures cannot fully explain differences that emerge during cycling. Mg recovery, soluble products and surface composition can indicate whether the benefit arises from easier ligand exchange, fewer side reactions or a more protective interphase. Solvent composition and electrode history must be controlled to distinguish these contributions.
After: Cycling can change the interface independently of the initial shell. Comparisons of carborane- and TFSI-based electrolytes follow this evolution alongside anion identity.[54] With solvent composition and electrode history controlled, Mg recovery, soluble products and surface analysis help distinguish fewer side reactions from improved protection. Combining these observations with exchange measurements tests whether ligand release also changes.

Before: 2.2. How coordinating anions can support reversible deposition
After: 2.2. Direct coordination and reversible deposition

Before: Chloride-based electrolytes show that direct anion coordination can be compatible with reversible Mg deposition. These coupled roles help explain why neither complete anion exclusion nor extensive contact pairing is a general design rule. The relevant comparison is between the reaction steps made accessible by each coordination environment.

An interaction that stabilises the initial state more strongly than the transition state raises this barrier, even if both states move down in energy. Before: 3.1. Compare energies for clearly defined reactions
After: 3.1. Free energies of defined reactions

Before: To establish whether anion coordination facilitates desolvation, the relevant free energies must be distinguished. Ion-pairing free energy describes the equilibrium between associated and dissociated ions. Ligand-exchange free energy compares states before and after one ligand replaces another. The activation barrier is the free-energy difference between the initial and transition states. Each calculation requires a balanced reaction with specified charge, solvent activity, composition and reference conditions. Association changes Mg-complex populations and reactivity.[23,32] Stabilising a complex can nevertheless raise its release barrier if the transition state is stabilised less. Association energy alone therefore cannot establish that an anion assists desolvation.
After: Evidence for anion-assisted desolvation must distinguish binding from reaction. Ion-pairing free energy describes the equilibrium between associated and dissociated ions. Ligand-exchange free energy compares states before and after one ligand replaces another. The activation barrier measures the free-energy difference between an initial state and its transition state. Each quantity refers to a different process and requires a balanced reaction with specified charge, solvent activity and reference conditions. Association changes both the population and reactivity of Mg complexes.[23,32] Stronger stabilisation of a complex can nevertheless increase its release barrier if the transition state is stabilised less. Association energy alone cannot resolve this possibility.

Before: Calculations should follow coordination changes rather than compare isolated cluster energies alone. When an anion replaces a solvent ligand, the reaction must include both the incoming anion and the released solvent. When a chelate opens, its conformations and their entropic contributions also matter. Comparing complexes of different charges requires a consistent chemical or electrode reservoir. These choices define the process represented by the calculated barrier. A proposed anion-assisted pathway is more convincing when it predicts a measurable change in ligand exchange or the potential dependence of Mg deposition.
After: A calculation is therefore most informative when it follows the coordination change proposed in the experiment. If an anion replaces a solvent ligand, both the incoming anion and the departing solvent belong in the reaction balance. If a chelate opens, its accessible conformations and their entropic contributions matter. Comparisons between complexes of different charges also need a consistent chemical or electrode reservoir. These choices define the meaning of the calculated barrier. A useful pathway should then predict an observable consequence, such as altered ligand exchange or a different potential dependence of Mg deposition.

Before: Enhanced sampling connects coordination changes to free-energy surfaces.[92–93] Suitable coordinates include the numbers of solvent and anion contacts and the distance from the electrode. A single coordinate may miss an alternative ligand-release pathway. Reweighting can estimate equilibrium properties where sampled distributions overlap, but cannot recover an unsampled transition.[94] Adsorption and reduction also depend on electrode potential and require an appropriate constant-potential or grand-canonical treatment.[31,95] Barriers should be compared for consistently defined reactions, with sampling uncertainty reported alongside the predicted experimental trends.
After: Enhanced sampling can connect these coordination changes to free-energy surfaces.[92–93] Solvent and anion contact numbers, together with distance from the electrode, provide possible reaction coordinates. More than one coordinate may be needed to capture alternative release pathways. Reweighting can recover equilibrium properties where sampled distributions overlap, but cannot reconstruct a transition that was never sampled.[94] Adsorption and reduction introduce electrode-potential dependence and call for an appropriate constant-potential or grand-canonical treatment.[31,95] Reporting the reaction definition and sampling uncertainty is essential when using a calculated barrier to explain an experimental trend.

Before: 3.2. Identify the magnesium species present in the electrolyte
After: 3.2. Mg speciation in the liquid and near the electrode

Before: Testing anion-assisted desolvation requires evidence that the proposed Mg complex is present. Raman and IR spectroscopy distinguish donor and anion environments, while ²⁵Mg NMR combined with computation provides information on Mg solvation and dynamics.[96] Studies across electrolyte compositions illustrate the value of combining these methods.[57–58,74,97] Assignments should distinguish donor atoms from ligand molecules, particularly for multidentate ligands. The measured species distribution provides a basis for kinetic analysis, although spectroscopy does not directly determine the barriers to the subsequent reactions.
After: The proposed reactive complex must first be identified in the electrolyte. Raman and IR spectra distinguish donor and anion environments, while ²⁵Mg NMR combined with computation can resolve aspects of Mg solvation and dynamics.[96] Measurements across electrolyte compositions show the value of combining these methods.[57–58,74,97] For multidentate ligands, an assignment must distinguish the number of donor atoms from the number of ligand molecules. Spectroscopy then establishes which environments are present; it does not, on its own, determine how rapidly those environments undergo desolvation.

Before: NMR methods must be selected according to the exchange time scale and spectral resolution. Quadrupolar broadening and low sensitivity complicate ²⁵Mg measurements. When bound and free ligand environments are resolved, EXSY can probe their exchange, provided that exchange cross-peaks are distinguished from nuclear Overhauser effects. DOSY provides information on diffusion and association but does not independently measure ligand-release rates. Similarly, Raman intensities cannot be converted into species populations without appropriate response factors. Combining these measurements helps resolve assignments that would remain ambiguous with a single technique.
After: The choice of NMR experiment depends on the exchange time scale and whether the relevant environments can be resolved. Quadrupolar broadening and low sensitivity make ²⁵Mg particularly demanding. Where bound and free ligands give distinct signals, EXSY can probe exchange, provided that nuclear Overhauser effects are distinguished from exchange cross-peaks. DOSY instead constrains diffusion and association, not ligand-release rates. Raman intensities likewise need appropriate response factors before they can be interpreted as populations. These limitations favour complementary measurements over a detailed assignment from one spectrum.

Before: The charge of Mg complexes also affects transport, particularly in chloride-containing and mixed-salt electrolytes.[60,82,98] Electrolytes with the same total Mg concentration can differ in conductivity because the complexes differ in charge, size and abundance. Mass spectrometry and crystallography can identify possible complexes, although ionisation and crystallisation may favour species that are less abundant in the liquid. Conversely, a minor species in the bulk may contribute substantially to deposition at a polarised electrode. Establishing that contribution requires a deposition response consistent with its proposed potential-dependent reactivity; detecting the complex outside the operating interface is insufficient.
After: Complex charge adds another layer to the interpretation, particularly in chloride-containing and mixed-salt electrolytes.[60,82,98] Two liquids with the same total Mg concentration may contain complexes of different charge, size and abundance, and consequently show different transport behaviour. Mass spectrometry and crystallography help identify possible structures, but ionisation or crystallisation can favour species that are scarce in solution. Conversely, a minor bulk species may contribute substantially to deposition at a polarised electrode. Its importance must be established through an electrochemical response consistent with its proposed reactivity, rather than its detection alone.

Before: Claims that anions are excluded from the first solvation shell require similar care. Neither a bulky anion nor a shifted vibrational band establishes the complete absence of Mg–anion contact. Reporting the associated fraction and its uncertainty allows a more meaningful comparison between formulations. Measurements of ligand exchange can then show whether changing this fraction also changes coordination dynamics, while Mg recovery establishes the electrochemical outcome. If the surface changes during the same experiment, additional controls are needed to distinguish the effects of solution coordination from those of interphase evolution.
After: Anion exclusion requires the same level of care. A bulky anion or a shifted vibrational band does not establish that every Mg–anion contact has disappeared. An associated fraction with an uncertainty estimate is more useful than a binary assignment of “present” or “absent”. Exchange measurements can then show whether changing that fraction alters coordination dynamics. Mg recovery provides the electrochemical outcome. If the surface evolves during the comparison, its contribution must be assessed before assigning the response to solution coordination.

Before: These measurements address three questions: which Mg complexes are present, how rapidly their ligands exchange, and whether they produce Mg or consume electrolyte. Speciation, exchange kinetics and the current associated with Mg deposition must therefore be interpreted together. For anion-assisted desolvation, a useful test is to reduce the population of the proposed active complex and examine whether exchange and deposition change as predicted. This can help distinguish a molecular contribution from suppressed decomposition or changes at the metal surface.
After: Together, these measurements establish which Mg complexes are present, how rapidly their ligands exchange and which reactions they undergo. Figure 3 separates these observables because none can substitute for the others. For example, reducing the abundance of a proposed active complex should change exchange and deposition in the direction predicted by the mechanism. A different response would point towards an alternative species, surface protection or suppressed decomposition. Such a perturbation tests the chemical explanation more directly than confirming the same shell assignment with several techniques.

Before: 3.3. Relate ligand exchange to magnesium deposition kinetics
After: 3.3. Ligand exchange and Mg deposition rates

Before: Faster bulk ligand exchange does not necessarily lead to faster Mg deposition. Diffusion, adsorption, electron transfer and nucleation also contribute, and their importance changes with potential and surface history. Exchange-sensitive NMR, temperature-dependent measurements and molecular dynamics can help determine whether ligand release contributes to the observed rate. Interpreting a relaxation time requires a model that relates the signal to ligand departure. The model must distinguish exchange by the dominant complex from exchange by a minor species that may account for much of the deposition current.
After: Ligand exchange becomes relevant to electrolyte design when it can be connected to Mg deposition. Faster exchange in the bulk need not increase deposition at the electrode, where diffusion, adsorption, electron transfer and nucleation also contribute. Their relative importance changes with potential and surface history. Exchange-sensitive NMR, temperature-dependent measurements and molecular dynamics can test whether ligand release affects the observed rate. The underlying model must specify which exchange process produces the signal and whether it belongs to the dominant complex or to a minor, more reactive species.

Before: Ligand residence times require an explicit definition. Brief departure followed by rebinding is treated differently in continuous and intermittent analyses. The distance cutoff, correlation function, rebinding treatment and sampling duration should therefore be reported. Diffusion calculations require convergence and finite-size checks,[99] whereas conductivity must account for correlated ion motion. These distinctions matter because improved conductivity can reduce polarisation without accelerating ligand release. Controlling for transport helps establish whether a change in Mg deposition rate arises from faster exchange.
After: Even a ligand residence time depends on its definition. A brief departure followed by rebinding counts differently in continuous and intermittent analyses. Distance cutoffs, correlation functions, treatment of rebinding and sampling duration should therefore accompany reported values. Diffusion calculations also need convergence and finite-size checks,[99] while conductivity depends on correlated ion motion. These are not interchangeable measures of desolvation. Improved transport can lower cell polarisation without accelerating ligand release, so transport must be characterised independently when relating exchange to deposition.

Before: Impedance and current transients can help identify the step affected by anion coordination. Frequency alone cannot distinguish film transport, electron transfer and diffusion, whose responses may overlap with adsorption, nucleation and surface evolution. Potential- and temperature-dependent measurements, transport data and Mg deposition current provide stronger constraints. Electron-transfer kinetics depend on reorganisation,[100] while Mg deposition also changes coordination and the metal surface. Faster exchange and deposition with little change in film response support a molecular contribution. Improved deposition at unchanged exchange rates during surface activation instead points to an interphase contribution.
After: Impedance and current transients add information about the interfacial response, although a frequency range cannot uniquely identify film transport, electron transfer or diffusion. Adsorption, nucleation and an evolving surface can produce overlapping signals. Potential and temperature dependence, transport measurements and the current associated with Mg deposition provide additional constraints. Electron transfer depends on reorganisation,[100] and Mg deposition also involves coordination changes and metal growth. Consistent changes in exchange and deposition, with little change in the film response, support a molecular contribution. Improvement that instead follows surface activation while exchange remains unchanged supports an interphase contribution.

Before: Binding energy is therefore unlikely to correlate universally with CE. CE compares the charge recovered during stripping with the charge passed during plating, whereas an exchange barrier describes one molecular step. Faster ligand release may leave adsorption or incorporation limiting. Conversely, suppressing decomposition can improve CE without changing exchange. A more informative comparison measures exchange and Mg deposition after a controlled change in donor identity or potential. If both respond as predicted, the descriptor gains support within that chemical system. Different responses indicate that the mechanism must account for another process.
After: CE answers a different question. It compares the charge recovered during stripping with the charge passed during plating, whereas an exchange barrier describes a molecular reaction step. Suppressing decomposition can increase CE without changing exchange, and faster ligand release may leave adsorption or metal incorporation limiting. A universal correlation between binding energy and CE is therefore unlikely. A more useful test asks whether a controlled change in donor identity or potential produces the predicted changes in both exchange and Mg deposition. Agreement supports the descriptor within that system; disagreement identifies a missing process.

Before: Figure 3. Complementary measurements distinguish Mg speciation, ligand exchange and reaction selectivity. a) Schematic coordination motifs illustrate possible Mg complexes. b) One-for-one exchange conserves L and L*; other donors are omitted for clarity. The decay curve illustrates a correlation function and contains no experimental data. c) Mg deposition competes with electrolyte reduction; the equation represents the net two-electron balance. Comparisons require consistent composition, temperature, potential and surface history.
After: Figure 3. Complementary measurements connect Mg speciation, ligand exchange and reaction selectivity. a) Illustrative coordination motifs and spectra represent the identification of Mg environments. The spectra contain no measured peak positions or quantitative population assignments. b) One-for-one exchange conserves L and L*, where L* denotes a distinguishable neutral ligand rather than a radical; other ligands are omitted. The correlation decay is schematic. c) Cathodic charge can produce Mg or drive electrolyte reduction. Mg recovery and product balances distinguish these outcomes; chemical corrosion must be assessed separately. Comparisons require controlled composition, temperature, potential and surface history. Mg²⁺ labels the metal centre rather than the net complex charge.

Before: 3.4. Determine reaction selectivity and the fate of the anion
After: 3.4. Reaction selectivity and anion consumption

Before: An anion that facilitates ligand release is beneficial only if subsequent reactions favour Mg deposition over decomposition. Calculations identify chelation-induced instability at the electrode/electrolyte interface and potential-dependent solvent decomposition in the double layer as competing processes.[30–31] Electron transfer requires electronic coupling, but not complete desolvation or direct adsorption of every reacting molecule. Orbital energies indicate susceptibility to reduction; product formation also depends on liquid reorganisation, bond cleavage and activation barriers. A cathodic onset alone therefore cannot distinguish Mg deposition from electrolyte reduction. The deposited metal and accompanying products must also be measured.
After: Facilitating ligand release helps only if the subsequent chemistry favours Mg deposition. Calculations identify chelation-induced instability and potential-dependent solvent decomposition in the double layer as competing processes.[30–31] Electron transfer needs electronic coupling, but neither complete desolvation nor direct adsorption of every reacting molecule is a universal prerequisite. Orbital energies describe one aspect of reduction susceptibility; liquid reorganisation, bond cleavage and activation barriers also determine products. A cathodic onset consequently cannot distinguish Mg deposition from electrolyte reduction. That assignment needs measurements of the deposited metal and accompanying products.

Before: Quantifying deposited Mg, recovered charge, gas, soluble products and film growth helps distinguish deposition from side reactions. Instantaneous Mg deposition current differs from cycle-integrated CE, and chemical corrosion can consume Mg without contributing to the deposition current. These distinctions are relevant to both early plating studies and later interphase work.[3,78,101] Operando EQCM-D measures changes in coupled mass and dissipation during conditioning and passivation.[102] Solvent coupling, porosity and changing surface area also affect the signal, so mass uptake cannot automatically be assigned to a compact SEI.
After: A material balance can separate these outcomes. Deposited Mg and recovered charge should be considered together with gas, soluble products and film growth. The instantaneous current producing Mg differs from cycle-integrated CE, and chemical corrosion consumes Mg without contributing to that deposition current. Both early plating studies and later interphase work make these distinctions relevant.[3,78,101] Operando EQCM-D follows changes in coupled mass and dissipation during conditioning and passivation.[102] Because solvent coupling, porosity and surface area also affect the signal, mass gain cannot be assigned automatically to a compact SEI.

Before: Product analysis is equally important for determining anion fate. An intact anion may simply be a spectator, while a sustained benefit may depend on gradual consumption from a large reservoir. Repeated assistance requires evidence that the recovered anion retains its kinetic effect under controlled surface conditions. Table 2 summarises experiments that can distinguish these possibilities. The contributions can coexist: an anion may facilitate solvent release, suppress a competing reduction and later form a film. Resolving these effects explains why anion coordination can be beneficial beyond SEI formation.
After: Anion recovery is equally important. An intact anion may be a spectator, while a benefit sustained for many cycles may still rely on slow consumption from a large reservoir. Repeated molecular assistance requires the recovered species to retain its kinetic effect under controlled surface conditions. Table 2 sets out experiments that distinguish these possibilities. The contributions can coexist: the same anion may facilitate solvent release, suppress a competing reduction and later form a film. Resolving when each occurs gives the desolvation argument its practical value.

Before: 4. Design Principles for Magnesium–Anion–Solvent Interactions
After: 4. Designing Magnesium–Anion–Solvent Interactions

Before: 4.1. Balance coordination stability and desolvation kinetics
After: 4.1. Coordination that permits ligand release

Before: Electrolyte design should balance the coordination needed to dissolve and transport Mg with the ligand rearrangement required for deposition. Solvent redesign, amine cosolvents and phosphate-containing formulations illustrate how coordination affects desolvation and interfacial reactions.[76,79,87,103] Depending on the initial environment, either increasing or decreasing anion coordination can improve Mg reversibility.[24,80] We therefore favour selecting anions for their influence on Mg–solvent interactions and ligand release. Their participation is beneficial when it facilitates deposition without forming persistent complexes or promoting decomposition. The design target is a favourable reaction sequence rather than a prescribed shell composition.
After: A useful Mg electrolyte must stabilise dissolved species without making their next reaction prohibitively slow. Solvent redesign, amine cosolvents and phosphate-containing formulations illustrate how coordination affects both desolvation and interfacial chemistry.[76,79,87,103] Depending on the starting environment, either greater or weaker anion coordination can improve Mg reversibility.[24,80] We therefore propose selecting anions for the ligand-release step they can facilitate. The useful interaction may displace a strongly bound solvent, permit a chelate to open or stabilise a rearranged intermediate. Its benefit is lost if the resulting complex remains trapped or decomposes before Mg can be deposited.

Before: Ligand denticity and steric structure influence how desolvation proceeds. A chelating ligand can dissociate through sequential loss of its donor contacts, while mixed solvents provide alternative environments during ligand exchange. Steric effects and competition between ether donors thus offer ways to facilitate desolvation beyond simply reducing donor affinity.[52] Fluoride boronic esters and strategies that jointly modify solvation and the interface provide further approaches.[104–106] However, similar cycling performance does not establish the same elementary reaction or a universal optimum coordination number.
After: Denticity and steric structure help determine which release sequence is accessible. A chelate can open through successive loss of donor contacts, while mixed solvents provide alternative coordination environments during exchange. Competition between ether donors and steric effects thus offer design variables beyond donor affinity alone.[52] Fluoride boronic esters and approaches that jointly modify solvation and the interface provide other routes.[104–106] These strategies may achieve similar cycling performance through different elementary steps. A successful formulation should therefore be associated with a proposed release sequence, rather than treated as evidence for one optimum coordination number.

Before: Interactions outside the first shell also influence desolvation. A cosolvent can alter anion availability and Mg–solvent binding without becoming a major Mg ligand. In amine-containing electrolytes, coordination and trace ionisation generate electrochemically active species,[84] while activation studies connect changes in these species with hydride-containing interfaces.[91] A single stable cluster cannot capture these coupled processes. Identifying the interacting species, exchange behaviour and reaction products helps distinguish outer-shell effects from direct anion coordination.
After: The surrounding liquid offers additional control. A cosolvent can change anion availability or Mg–solvent binding without becoming a major first-shell ligand. In amine-containing electrolytes, coordination and trace ionisation generate electrochemically active species,[84] while activation studies connect changes in those species with hydride-containing interfaces.[91] A single stable cluster cannot represent this evolving chemistry. Following speciation, exchange and products across the treatment reveals whether the benefit comes from direct anion binding, interactions outside the shell or changes in surface activation.

Before: A meaningful comparison starts with a proposed coordination environment and a control designed to test its role in desolvation. Association and transport measurements should be combined with ligand exchange and the initial Mg deposition response on comparable surfaces. Changing the potential or donor composition is particularly informative when the mechanism predicts a reversal in relative reaction rates. The highest CE at an intermediate composition may reflect competing processes. Predicting how this optimum shifts with conditions provides stronger mechanistic support than identifying it alone.
After: The first design experiment should test the proposed coordination change against a deliberately chosen control. Association and transport measurements establish what changes in solution; exchange and initial Mg deposition on comparable surfaces test the kinetic consequence. Changing donor composition or potential is especially informative if the mechanism predicts that the ordering of reaction rates will reverse. An intermediate composition may give the highest CE because several processes compete. Predicting how that optimum moves with conditions provides stronger evidence than finding it in a single series.

Before: Mixed-salt electrolytes provide a practical way to vary anion availability. Magnesium triflate formulations and tetrabutylammonium triflate additives have enabled reversible cycling in otherwise poorly reversible electrolytes.[107–108] A non-Mg salt can vary anion concentration at fixed total Mg concentration, although the accompanying cation and changes in ionic strength require controls. Speciation measurements should account for all added ions. In Li-containing mixtures, for example, Li may also participate in cathode reactions, complicating attribution of the measured improvement to anion coordination.
After: Mixed salts make such perturbations possible. Magnesium triflate formulations and tetrabutylammonium triflate additives have enabled reversible cycling in otherwise poorly reversible liquids.[107–108] A non-Mg salt can vary anion concentration while keeping total Mg fixed. The added counter-cation and the accompanying change in ionic strength remain part of the experiment, however, and need controls. Speciation analysis should include all added ions. In Li-containing mixtures, Li may also participate at the cathode, so an increase in capacity cannot automatically be attributed to improved Mg desolvation.

Before: 4.2. Maintain an interface that supports reversible Mg deposition
After: 4.2. Desolvation at an evolving Mg surface

Before: Facilitating desolvation is useful only if the Mg surface remains electrochemically active. Adsorption, suppressed solvent reduction, removal of passivating compounds and protective interphases can support sustained Mg plating and stripping.[20,109–111] Artificial interfaces and electrolyte additives provide further control.[112–113] A perfluorinated pinacolatoaluminate salt, for example, uses anion–solvent coordination to promote a beneficial interphase.[114] This supports an interphase contribution but does not establish faster release of Mg-bound ligands. Tests of a solution-phase desolvation mechanism must therefore account for surface changes caused by the same formulation.
After: Molecular design has to be reconciled with the surface on which deposition occurs. Adsorption, suppressed solvent reduction, removal of passivating compounds and protective interphases can each help sustain Mg plating/stripping.[20,109–111] Artificial interfaces and additives provide further ways to control that surface.[112–113] A perfluorinated pinacolatoaluminate salt, for example, uses anion–solvent coordination to promote a beneficial interphase.[114] The result supports an interphase contribution without establishing faster release of Mg-bound ligands. Any claim for solution-assisted desolvation in such a formulation must account for the surface changes produced by the same chemistry.

Before: Electrolyte conditioning can obscure this distinction. Controlled H₂O/Cl⁻ experiments demonstrate the contribution of surface passivation to Mg reversibility.[115] Operando EQCM-D measurements further show the formation and removal of contaminant-associated layers during conditioning in the investigated borate electrolytes. In the TFSI systems examined in the same study, chloride accelerates the dissolution of passivating layers even without an applied current.[102] A water-scavenging additive can eliminate the need for conditioning,[116] while triphenolate–borohydride salts provide a separate mixed-salt route to reversible cycling.[117] Analysing the solution and activation products before and after treatment is therefore necessary to identify the electrolyte species responsible for the observed behaviour.
After: Conditioning makes this separation particularly important. Controlled H₂O/Cl⁻ experiments demonstrate the effect of surface passivation on Mg reversibility.[115] Operando EQCM-D reveals formation and removal of contaminant-associated layers during conditioning in the borate electrolytes investigated. In the TFSI systems examined in the same study, chloride accelerates dissolution of passivating layers even without an applied current.[102] A water-scavenging additive can remove the need for conditioning,[116] whereas triphenolate–borohydride salts provide a distinct mixed-salt route to reversible cycling.[117] Comparing the liquid and activation products before and after treatment helps identify which species, rather than which nominal starting composition, supports deposition.

Before: The composition of an interphase alone does not reveal how Mg crosses it. Borohydride-derived, gradient and hybrid interphases illustrate different approaches to sustaining Mg transfer.[20,118–119] A multifunctional diamine also combines an in situ cross-linked gel with an Mg–N-containing interphase for operation at elevated temperature.[120] In such heterogeneous layers, transport may occur through defects, phase boundaries, other components or exposed regions of the metal. Phase analysis should therefore be considered together with resistance changes and Mg recovery. In particular, detecting a hydride or nitride does not establish that its bulk phase provides the dominant transport pathway.
After: Interphase composition must also be connected to function. Borohydride-derived, gradient and hybrid layers provide different routes to sustained Mg transfer.[20,118–119] A multifunctional diamine combines an in situ cross-linked gel with an Mg–N-containing interphase for elevated-temperature operation.[120] Such layers are heterogeneous. Mg may cross through defects, phase boundaries, other components or exposed regions of metal. Identifying a hydride or nitride therefore does not establish transport through its bulk phase. Phase analysis becomes more informative when accompanied by resistance changes and Mg recovery during operation.

Before: Changes in deposit morphology can improve cycling independently of desolvation. Surface kinetic control, scaffolds, exposed facets, horizontal platelets and orientation-selective additives influence nucleation and current distribution.[121–125] Studies of diffusion-dependent growth and dendrite formation in glyme electrolytes also show that Mg is not intrinsically immune to nonuniform deposition.[126–127] Comparisons at matched capacity, transport conditions and substrate preparation are needed to separate these effects from ligand release. A smoother deposit is therefore insufficient evidence for improved desolvation; the proposed coordination change should also explain the morphology under otherwise comparable conditions.
After: Deposit growth introduces a further contribution. Surface kinetic control, scaffolds, exposed facets, horizontal platelets and orientation-selective additives change nucleation and current distribution.[121–125] Diffusion-dependent growth and dendrite formation in glyme electrolytes also demonstrate that Mg is not intrinsically immune to nonuniform deposition.[126–127] A smoother deposit may improve cycling without any change in ligand-release kinetics. To connect morphology to desolvation, comparisons should retain the same capacity, transport conditions and substrate preparation, and the proposed coordination mechanism should explain the growth response under those conditions.

Before: Water, oxygen and impurities introduced with the salt must likewise be treated as variables in the mechanism. The water tolerance of an AlCl₃/MgCl₂/Mg(TFSI)₂ formulation is specific to that electrolyte and does not establish a general impurity threshold.[128] Changing the solvent can alter impurity uptake or conditioning reactions as well as Mg binding. Water measurements with a clearly defined ppm basis, documented handling and halide controls are consequently important. Comparing dry and deliberately dosed electrolytes on fresh and conditioned Mg can help determine whether changes in spectra, gas evolution and current arise from the intended solvation change or from impurity-induced surface reactions.
After: Impurities can alter both the liquid and the surface, making them part of the mechanism rather than a minor experimental detail. The water tolerance reported for an AlCl₃/MgCl₂/Mg(TFSI)₂ formulation is specific to that system.[128] A solvent change may alter impurity uptake or conditioning chemistry as well as Mg binding. Water content with a stated ppm basis, handling conditions and halide controls are therefore needed to interpret the comparison. Testing dry and deliberately dosed liquids on fresh and conditioned Mg can reveal whether spectra, gas evolution and current follow the intended solvation change or an impurity-induced surface reaction.

Before: We propose comparing the original and modified electrolytes on fresh and preconditioned Mg, using a common preconditioning protocol and characterising the initial surface. Substrate preparation, capacity and temperature should be matched. Compare Mg deposition rates at matched potential, or overpotentials at matched current, while controlling transport and ohmic losses. Electrolyte replacement further distinguishes solution and surface effects if the preformed interphase remains intact; its dissolution makes activity loss difficult to interpret. Section 5 extends this approach to a composition series, with significant differences determined from replicate measurements.
After: We suggest a paired comparison of the original and modified liquids on fresh Mg and on Mg prepared by a common preconditioning protocol. The initial surface should be characterised, with substrate preparation, capacity and temperature matched. Mg deposition rates can be compared at the same potential, or overpotentials at the same current, after accounting for transport and ohmic losses. Replacing the liquid on a conditioned electrode then tests whether the benefit remains with the surface. Film integrity must be checked: loss of activity after film dissolution cannot distinguish a solution effect from destruction of protection. Section 5 extends this comparison to a composition series with replicate measurements.

Before: 4.3. Evaluate anion effects at the cathode
After: 4.3. Coordination and cathode compatibility

Before: An electrolyte that supports Mg deposition must also be compatible with the cathode. Coordination changes can facilitate desolvation, but the same electrolyte may oxidise, corrode the current collector or dissolve active material. Boron-based, non-nucleophilic and fluorinated dialkoxide electrolytes address aspects of this compatibility problem,[129–133] as does high-voltage phenolic electrolyte design.[134] Depending on the cathode, desolvation and charge transfer may be followed by ion diffusion, phase transformation or conversion. Coordination strategies must therefore be assessed at both electrodes, including the associated chemical losses.
After: The cathode places a second set of requirements on the same electrolyte. A coordination change that facilitates Mg deposition may also promote oxidation, current-collector corrosion or dissolution of active material. Boron-based, non-nucleophilic and fluorinated dialkoxide electrolytes address different parts of this problem,[129–133] as does high-voltage phenolic electrolyte design.[134] At the cathode, desolvation and charge transfer can precede ion diffusion, a phase transition or a conversion reaction. Anion selection therefore has to account for the host chemistry and the associated material losses as well as the Mg-metal interface.

Before: CuSe provides an example of anion coordination influencing cathode behaviour.[135] Adding OTf⁻ changes the assigned Mg solvation environment from [Mg(DME)₃]²⁺ to the anion-containing average composition [Mg(DME)₂.₅OTf]⁺. The authors associate this change with easier desolvation and faster cathode charge transfer, reporting an increase in capacity from 228 to 357 mAh g⁻¹ at 0.1 A g⁻¹. The comparison concerns cathode capacity within the same study, rather than Mg deposition performance. Here, anion incorporation refers to the solvation shell, not OTf⁻ insertion into CuSe; the fractional ligand number denotes an average environment. Resolving phase evolution remains necessary to distinguish faster interfacial transfer from changes in the solid-state conversion reaction.
After: CuSe illustrates a direct link between solvation and cathode response.[135] Adding OTf⁻ changes the assigned Mg environment from [Mg(DME)₃]²⁺ to the anion-containing average composition [Mg(DME)₂.₅OTf]⁺. The authors associate this change with easier desolvation and faster cathode charge transfer, and report a capacity increase from 228 to 357 mAh g⁻¹ at 0.1 A g⁻¹. These values compare cathode performance within that study, not Mg deposition efficiency. The anion enters the solvation shell; the assignment does not imply OTf⁻ insertion into CuSe, and the fractional ligand number represents an average environment. Phase-resolved measurements are needed to determine whether improved interfacial transfer also changes the conversion reaction.

Before: Organic cathodes further illustrate the importance of identifying the species involved in storage. In a Mg-FPB/quinone battery, ATR-IR supports carbonyl reduction and coordination with Mg²⁺, while incompletely dissociated MgFPB⁺ ion pairs are also detected.[136] Anion association can therefore affect which Mg species are available for storage, as well as the energy required for desolvation. Polymer-based storage and enolisation reactions provide additional, chemically distinct examples.[137–138] Measurements at matched states of charge are needed to identify the stored species and any limitations imposed by the host reaction. Capacity alone cannot distinguish improved interfacial transfer from changes in the solid-state reaction or participation of another ion.
After: Organic cathodes raise a related question about the species involved in storage. In a Mg-FPB/quinone battery, ATR-IR supports carbonyl reduction and Mg²⁺ coordination, while incompletely dissociated MgFPB⁺ ion pairs are also detected.[136] Association can thus affect the available Mg species as well as the energy needed to remove ligands. Polymer-based storage and enolisation reactions provide chemically distinct examples.[137–138] Measurements at comparable states of charge can identify which species are stored and where the host reaction becomes limiting. Capacity alone cannot separate improved interfacial transfer from a different storage reaction or participation of another ion.

Before: Sulfur cathodes highlight the consequences of stabilising reactive species in solution. Electrolyte compatibility with sulfur was already a central consideration in an early Mg–S demonstration.[139] More recently, an MOEA-containing Mg(OTf)₂–MgCl₂/DME electrolyte was tested with Mo₆S₈, CuS and S–CNT cathodes, extending donor modification to several sulfur-containing chemistries.[89] Solvation that facilitates the conversion of soluble intermediates can also increase active-material loss or shuttling to the Mg electrode. The aim is therefore to support reversible conversion while limiting these losses. Separate measurements of dissolved cathode species and electrolyte decomposition products are needed to evaluate that balance.
After: Sulfur cathodes expose the trade-off between reactive solution species and material retention. Electrolyte compatibility was central to an early Mg–S demonstration.[139] An MOEA-containing Mg(OTf)₂–MgCl₂/DME electrolyte has more recently been tested with Mo₆S₈, CuS and S–CNT cathodes, extending donor modification across several sulfur-containing chemistries.[89] Solvation that aids conversion through soluble intermediates may also increase dissolution or shuttling to Mg. The design task is to preserve the useful reaction while limiting those losses. Quantifying dissolved cathode species separately from electrolyte decomposition products is necessary to establish that balance.

Before: These effects can be examined at matched cathode loading, capacity and state of charge. Interfacial measurements should accompany phase analysis and quantification of dissolved active material and electrolyte products. Faster kinetics with comparable phase evolution support an interfacial contribution. Dissolution changes or storage of an added cation must also be considered; in mixed-metal electrolytes, elemental and charge balances help identify the ions involved. Testing Mg deposition after cathode exposure then reveals whether the proposed benefit survives chemical cross-talk between the electrodes.
After: Cathode comparisons should therefore match loading, capacity and state of charge while following phase evolution, interfacial response and dissolved products. Faster kinetics with similar phase evolution support an interfacial contribution. A change in dissolution or the participation of an added cation offers a different explanation; mixed-metal electrolytes require elemental and charge balances to identify the stored ions. Finally, testing Mg deposition after cathode exposure reveals whether the molecular benefit survives chemical cross-talk between the electrodes.

Before: The oxidation onset is an initial indicator of electrolyte stability, but it does not fully describe decomposition at the cathode interface.[140–141] Its measured value depends on electrode area, scan rate and the current threshold. We therefore recommend voltage-hold measurements at the intended porous cathode to assess sustained decomposition and resistance growth. Full-cell comparisons should also specify Mg excess, electrolyte volume, cathode loading and capacity limits. Before: 6. Conclusions and Outlook
After: 6. Conclusions and Outlook

Before: 6.1. Recognizing the desolvation role of coordinated anions
After: 6.1. Anion coordination beyond SEI formation

Before: Anions in the first solvation shell can contribute directly to Mg²⁺ desolvation, beyond supplying decomposition products for an SEI. By changing Mg–solvent interactions and the sequence of ligand rearrangement and release, a suitable anion can make Mg deposition more accessible. This benefit depends on the reaction pathway: persistent coordination may instead hinder release, while weak ion pairing can improve deposition by increasing the supply of reactive Mg species.[24–25,80] Anion selection should therefore consider the desolvation step it can facilitate, together with its tendency to undergo side reactions or form an interphase. Establishing whether the anion is released, regenerated or consumed helps explain how long the benefit can persist.
After: Anions in the first solvation shell can assist Mg²⁺ desolvation by changing Mg–solvent interactions and the sequence of ligand rearrangement and release. This molecular function extends beyond supplying decomposition products for an SEI. It also explains why the amount of anion coordination cannot, by itself, define a good electrolyte. Persistent binding can hinder release, whereas weak ion pairing may improve deposition by increasing the supply of reactive Mg species.[24–25,80] The central design question is which step a selected anion makes more accessible. Its stability, release and possible consumption then determine whether that benefit can persist during cycling.

Before: 6.2. Establishing which step anion coordination improves
After: 6.2. Establishing the molecular contribution

Before: The main experimental need is to connect changes in coordination with measured ligand-exchange rates and Mg deposition under controlled surface and impurity conditions. Species populations and reaction products are needed to distinguish easier desolvation from increased reactant availability or reduced electrolyte decomposition. A proposed mechanism should predict the response to changes in solvent, anion or potential, including conditions under which the benefit is lost. Computational and data-driven methods can help select these discriminating experiments, provided that their predictions are tested beyond the electrolyte family used to develop them.
After: The next advance requires a direct connection between a controlled coordination change and the kinetics of Mg deposition. Ligand-exchange measurements provide one part of this connection; species populations, surface state and reaction products provide the others. Together, they can distinguish easier desolvation from more available reactants or reduced electrolyte loss. A convincing mechanism should predict the response to a new donor, anion or potential, including conditions under which the benefit disappears. Computation and data-driven methods are most useful when they help select these discriminating tests and are evaluated beyond the compositions used to develop them.

Before: 6.3. Extending molecular design to practical cell operation
After: 6.3. Retaining the benefit in a working cell

Before: For anion-assisted desolvation to improve practical cells, the electrolyte must remain compatible with both electrodes and sustain cycling with limited Mg and electrolyte inventories.[6,147] Cathode reactions, interphase evolution and continuing electrolyte consumption must therefore be considered alongside the initial deposition kinetics. The next step is to establish how a selected coordination environment changes the reactions that control cell performance. Magnesium electrolyte discovery should progress from identifying favourable solvation structures to designing desolvation and interfacial reaction pathways that remain effective across formulations and operating conditions.
After: For anion-assisted desolvation to improve practical cells, the same electrolyte must remain compatible with both electrodes and sustain operation with limited Mg and electrolyte inventories.[6,147] Cathode reactions, interphase evolution and continuing electrolyte consumption determine whether an initially favourable molecular pathway remains useful. These constraints should guide anion selection from the outset. Future magnesium electrolytes should be designed around desolvation and interfacial reaction pathways whose benefits remain predictable across compositions and operating conditions.
